title: Chapter 10: Fiscal Policy, Automatic Stabilizers, and Sovereign Debt
benchmark: Paul Krugman & Robin Wells, Macroeconomics (Principles SSOT, Spring 2027)

questions.title: Core Tools of Federal Fiscal Policy
questions.prompt_template: Which set of policy instruments defines federal fiscal policy?

hints.text: Distinguish actions taken through the federal budget (Congress and the President) from actions taken by the central bank.
Look for the three fiscal variables that appear directly in the planned aggregate expenditure equation AE = C0 + c(Y - T + TR) + Ip + G + NX0.

options_template.text: Adjusting federal government purchases (G), transfer payments (TR), and taxation (T).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Fiscal policy consists of deliberate federal changes in government purchases, transfer payments, and taxes to influence aggregate demand, employment, and price stability.

options_template.text: Adjusting the interest on reserve balances (IORB) and conducting open-market bond operations.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monetary-Fiscal Confusion): Setting IORB and conducting open-market operations are monetary policy tools controlled by the Federal Reserve, not fiscal policy tools controlled by Congress and the President.

options_template.text: Regulating commercial bank capital ratios and setting private-sector minimum wages.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Regulatory vs. Fiscal Scope): Bank supervision and labor-market regulations are microeconomic or financial regulatory policies rather than federal fiscal policy instruments.

options_template.text: Fixing foreign exchange rates and imposing import tariffs exclusively to balance trade.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade Policy Conflation): Exchange-rate management and trade barriers belong to international trade and exchange-rate policy, not the core G, TR, and T instruments of fiscal stabilization.

questions.title: Identifying Expansionary Fiscal Policy
questions.prompt_template: Which combination of federal budget actions represents expansionary fiscal policy designed to close a recessionary gap?

hints.text: Expansionary fiscal policy aims to increase planned aggregate expenditure and shift the AD curve rightward.
Check how each instrument affects AD = C(Y - T + TR) + I + G + NX: higher G, higher TR, and lower T all push AD up.

options_template.text: Decreasing government purchases, decreasing transfer payments, and raising income tax rates.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy Direction Reversal): Cutting G and TR while raising T reduces aggregate demand and represents contractionary fiscal policy, which would worsen a recessionary gap.

options_template.text: Increasing government purchases, increasing transfer payments, or cutting taxes.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Raising G directly boosts aggregate demand, while raising TR or cutting T increases household disposable income (YD = Y - T + TR), stimulating consumption and shifting AD rightward.

options_template.text: Raising taxes and cutting transfer payments to eliminate the federal budget deficit immediately.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Procyclical Austerity): Raising taxes and cutting transfers contracts aggregate demand; balancing the budget during a slump is contractionary rather than expansionary.

options_template.text: Increasing government purchases while simultaneously cutting transfer payments by a larger amount.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Net Contraction Confusion): A larger cut in transfers than the increase in purchases can reduce net aggregate spending rather than delivering a clear expansionary stimulus.

questions.topic: Federal vs. State and Local Fiscal Capacity
questions.title: Why Countercyclical Fiscal Policy Is Primarily Federal
questions.prompt_template: Why is the federal government—rather than state and local governments—uniquely positioned to conduct countercyclical fiscal stabilization during a recession?

hints.text: Think about what happens to a state's budget when tax receipts drop during a recession.
Recall the legal budget rules that bind most state and local operating budgets compared with the federal government's borrowing capacity.

options_template.text: State and local governments are legally prohibited from collecting income or sales taxes during recessions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Misconception): States and municipalities continue collecting taxes during recessions; the problem is that their tax revenues fall automatically when incomes and sales drop.

options_template.text: Only state governments have access to the bond market to finance highway and school construction.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Borrowing Access Reversal): The federal government has the deepest borrowing capacity via U.S. Treasury securities, whereas states face strict constitutional borrowing limits on operating budgets.

options_template.text: Most state and local governments operate under balanced-budget rules that force them to cut spending or raise taxes when revenues fall in a downturn.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Balanced-budget requirements compel states to tighten budgets during recessions (procyclical behavior), whereas the federal government can run deliberate countercyclical deficits.

options_template.text: State and local spending does not count as part of government purchases (G) in the national expenditure identity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (GDP Accounting Error): State and local purchases of goods and services are included in G; the constraint is institutional balanced-budget rules, not GDP accounting.

questions.title: How Government Purchases Differ from Transfers and Taxes in AD
questions.prompt_template: In the aggregate expenditure framework AD = C + I + G + NX, how do changes in taxes (T) and transfer payments (TR) affect aggregate demand differently from direct government purchases (G)?

hints.text: Look at where G, T, and TR appear in the equation AE = C0 + c(Y - T + TR) + Ip + G + NX0.
Notice which variable is multiplied by the marginal propensity to consume c and which variable is not.

options_template.text: Taxes and transfers enter G directly, whereas government purchases alter household disposable income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Component Reversal): Direct government purchases enter G one-for-one; transfers and taxes are excluded from G and instead affect household disposable income YD = Y - T + TR.

options_template.text: Taxes and transfers shift the LRAS curve immediately, whereas government purchases shift only the AD curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (AD-LRAS Confusion): In the short run, all three fiscal tools operate primarily on aggregate demand; taxes and transfers do not instantly expand physical productive capacity.

options_template.text: Transfers are counted twice—once in G and once in C—so they have a larger initial impact than direct purchases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting Fallacy): Transfer payments are deliberately excluded from G to avoid double counting; they enter GDP only when recipients spend them on consumption C.

options_template.text: Government purchases enter AD directly one-for-one, whereas taxes and transfers act indirectly by changing household disposable income and consumption.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Every dollar of G is immediate demand for goods and services, while T and TR first change disposable income (YD = Y - T + TR), which alters consumption C by the MPC.

questions.title: Why the Purchases Multiplier Exceeds the Tax Multiplier
questions.prompt_template: Why is the government purchases multiplier (kG) strictly larger in absolute magnitude than the lump-sum tax multiplier (kT) whenever 0 < MPC < 1?

hints.text: Compare what happens in Round 1 when the government spends $100B directly versus when it cuts household taxes by $100B.
Compare the numerators of kG = 1/(1 - c) and |kT| = c/(1 - c) for any 0 < c < 1.

options_template.text: Because 100% of a change in G enters Round 1 spending, whereas households save a fraction (1 - c) of a tax cut before spending fraction c.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Direct purchases inject the full dollar amount into Round 1 of aggregate expenditure, while a tax cut first raises disposable income and experiences an immediate saving leakage of (1 - c).

options_template.text: Because tax cuts are subject to progressive income taxation, whereas government purchases are exempt from all taxes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-on-Tax Confusion): Even with pure lump-sum taxes (t = 0), |kG| = 1/(1 - c) exceeds |kT| = c/(1 - c) strictly because households save a portion (1 - c) of their tax cut in Round 1.

options_template.text: Because government purchases never crowd out private investment, whereas tax cuts always cause complete crowding out.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Crowding-Out Asymmetry): Deficit-financed spending and deficit-financed tax cuts both require Treasury borrowing; the multiplier gap between kG and kT arises from Round 1 saving leakage.

options_template.text: Because the tax multiplier equals 1/(1 - MPS), which is always smaller than 1/(1 - MPC).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Formula Distortion): The lump-sum tax multiplier is -MPC/(1 - MPC) = -c/(1 - c), not 1/(1 - MPS).

questions.title: Why an Equal Rise in G and T Remains Expansionary
questions.prompt_template: In a simple Keynesian model with lump-sum taxes and 0 < c < 1, why does an equal increase in government purchases and taxes (ΔG = ΔT > 0) still expand equilibrium output?

hints.text: Compare the Round 1 spending gain from +ΔG with the Round 1 consumption loss from +ΔT.
Add the algebraic formulas for kG = 1/(1 - c) and kT = -c/(1 - c).

options_template.text: Because households ignore lump-sum taxes completely and do not reduce consumption at all when taxes rise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero Consumption Response): Households do reduce consumption by c·ΔT in Round 1; the net expansion occurs because c·ΔT is smaller than ΔG, not because it is zero.

options_template.text: Because the government spends 100% of ΔG immediately while households reduce Round 1 consumption by only c·ΔT, leaving a net initial boost of (1 - c)ΔG that multiplies to ΔG.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Adding kG = 1/(1 - c) and kT = -c/(1 - c) yields kBB = (1 - c)/(1 - c) = 1, so the net expansion equals exactly ΔG regardless of the value of c.

options_template.text: Because a balanced-budget expansion lowers real interest rates and stimulates private investment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Interest-Rate Mechanism Confusion): Even at a fixed interest rate and fixed price level, the balanced-budget multiplier equals 1 purely from the Round 1 difference between ΔG and c·ΔT.

options_template.text: Because kBB equals 1/(1 - c) whenever the budget remains balanced.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplier Identity Error): 1/(1 - c) is the government purchases multiplier kG alone; subtracting the tax contraction -c/(1 - c) leaves kBB = 1.

questions.title: Defining Automatic Stabilizers
questions.prompt_template: What distinguishes an automatic stabilizer from discretionary fiscal policy?

hints.text: Focus on the word 'automatic'—does Congress have to vote on a new bill for the stabilizer to activate?
Recall how standing tax and transfer rules respond automatically when national income falls or rises.

options_template.text: Automatic stabilizers are controlled by the Federal Reserve rather than Congress.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Agency Confusion): Automatic stabilizers are federal fiscal laws (tax brackets and transfer programs) enacted by Congress, not central-bank monetary rules.

options_template.text: Automatic stabilizers require a new Act of Congress at the onset of every recession.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Discretionary Definition): Requiring new legislation is the defining feature of discretionary fiscal policy, not automatic stabilizers.

options_template.text: Automatic stabilizers are built-in tax and transfer rules in standing law that adjust countercyclically without new legislation.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because they are embedded in existing law, automatic stabilizers immediately cushion disposable income during downturns and restrain demand during booms without recognition or legislative lags.

options_template.text: Automatic stabilizers guarantee a balanced federal budget in every phase of the business cycle.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Balanced-Budget Myth): Automatic stabilizers intentionally widen the cyclical deficit during recessions and narrow it during booms to dampen GDP volatility.

questions.title: Classifying Automatic Stabilizers vs. Discretionary Actions
questions.prompt_template: Which pair consists exclusively of automatic stabilizers in the U.S. fiscal system?

hints.text: Ask which programs automatically expand payouts or reduce tax burdens the moment a worker loses a job or earns less income.
Eliminate any option that mentions a newly passed bill, one-time rebate, or Federal Reserve action.

options_template.text: A newly enacted federal highway construction bill and a one-time stimulus rebate check.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Discretionary Instruments): Both a new infrastructure bill and a one-time stimulus check require new congressional legislation and are therefore discretionary fiscal policy.

options_template.text: A temporary 10% income tax surcharge passed by Congress and an emergency defense appropriation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Discretionary Instruments): Both policies are deliberate legislative acts enacted in response to specific macroeconomic or geopolitical conditions.

options_template.text: Federal Reserve open-market purchases and a state-level constitutional balanced-budget mandate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Non-Stabilizer Mix): Open-market operations are monetary policy, and state balanced-budget mandates act procyclically rather than as automatic stabilizers.

options_template.text: Progressive personal income tax brackets and standing unemployment insurance (UI) benefits.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Progressive income taxes automatically collect less when incomes fall (and more during booms), while standing UI automatically pays more when layoffs rise, all without new legislation.

questions.title: Distinguishing Recognition, Legislative, and Implementation Lags
questions.prompt_template: After statistical agencies confirm a recession has begun, Congress spends four months negotiating tax brackets and spending priorities before passing a stimulus bill. Which fiscal policy lag does this four-month delay illustrate?

hints.text: Place the three lags in chronological order: spotting the problem, passing the law, and spending the money.
The prompt explicitly describes the time Congress spends negotiating and passing the bill.

options_template.text: Legislative lag.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The legislative lag is the time required for Congress and the President to negotiate, draft, and enact tax or spending legislation once a macroeconomic problem has been recognized.

options_template.text: Recognition lag.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lag Misidentification): The recognition lag is the earlier delay while agencies like the BEA and BLS collect and revise data so policymakers realize a downturn has started.

options_template.text: Implementation lag.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lag Misidentification): The implementation lag occurs after a bill is signed into law, while agencies award contracts, distribute grants, and put funds into circulation.

options_template.text: Crowding-out lag.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Invented Terminology): Crowding out is an interest-rate offset in the loanable funds market, not one of the three canonical timing lags of discretionary fiscal policy.

questions.title: Mechanism of Fiscal Crowding Out
questions.prompt_template: What is crowding out in macroeconomic fiscal policy?

hints.text: Trace how the U.S. Treasury finances a budget deficit and what happens in the loanable funds market.
Connect higher real interest rates (r) to business capital investment (I) and interest-sensitive household borrowing.

options_template.text: The increase in private consumption that occurs when households anticipate future tax cuts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Reversal): Crowding out refers to a reduction in private spending, not an increase.

options_template.text: The reduction in private investment (I) and interest-sensitive consumption (C) caused when deficit-financed government borrowing drives up real interest rates (r).
options_template.feedback: Correct. When the Treasury borrows in the loanable funds market to finance a deficit, higher demand for funds pushes up r, raising borrowing costs and reducing private investment and durable consumption.

options_template.text: The displacement of state government tax revenue when federal income tax rates are cut.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intergovernmental Confusion): Crowding out operates through higher real interest rates in credit markets reducing private-sector spending, not through state tax-base overlap.

options_template.text: The decline in federal tax collections caused by households falling into lower tax brackets during a recession.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stabilizer Confusion): Falling tax collections during a recession describe automatic stabilizers, not crowding out.

questions.title: Flow Variable vs. Stock Variable
questions.prompt_template: Which statement accurately distinguishes the federal budget deficit from the public (sovereign) debt?

hints.text: Recall the bathtub analogy: water flowing in per year is a flow, while total water currently in the tub is a stock.
Match the annual fiscal-year shortfall (outlays minus revenues) to flow and cumulative Treasury liabilities to stock.

options_template.text: The budget deficit is a stock measured at a point in time, while public debt is an annual flow.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stock-Flow Reversal): This reverses the two definitions; the deficit is an annual flow and public debt is a cumulative stock.

options_template.text: Both the budget deficit and public debt are flow variables measured per quarter.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Flow-Only Fallacy): Public debt is a cumulative stock measured at a specific date, not a flow per quarter.

options_template.text: The budget deficit is a flow equal to outlays minus revenues over a single fiscal year, whereas public debt is the cumulative stock of outstanding government liabilities at a point in time.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Over a fiscal year (Oct 1–Sep 30), outlays minus revenues yield the flow deficit, which adds to the cumulative stock of outstanding public debt.

options_template.text: Public debt equals total federal tax revenues collected since the country's founding.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Liability Confusion): Public debt reflects the cumulative sum of past deficits minus past surpluses—outstanding liabilities owed to bondholders—not cumulative tax revenues.

questions.title: Defining the Structural (Cyclically Adjusted) Deficit
questions.prompt_template: How do macroeconomists define the structural (cyclically adjusted) budget deficit?

hints.text: Think about what remains of the federal deficit once the business cycle is neither in a recession nor in an overheating boom.
When Y = Yp, the cyclical balance equals $0; what is the remaining budget gap called?

options_template.text: The temporary portion of a budget deficit caused automatically when real GDP falls below potential GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cyclical-Structural Swap): The temporary deficit caused by Y < Yp is the cyclical deficit, not the structural deficit.

options_template.text: The portion of the federal deficit financed exclusively by foreign central banks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ownership Conflation): Whether bonds are held domestically or abroad does not define structural vs. cyclical deficits; the distinction depends on the output gap.

options_template.text: The total interest paid on outstanding Treasury securities during a single fiscal year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Interest-Only Confusion): Interest outlays are part of total outlays, but the structural deficit measures the full budget shortfall evaluated at Y = Yp.

options_template.text: The underlying budget deficit that would persist even if the economy were operating at full-employment potential output (Y = Yp).
options_template.feedback: Correct. At full employment (Y = Yp), the cyclical balance is zero, so the entire observed deficit equals the structural deficit reflecting baseline tax and spending laws.

questions.title: Separating Primary Outlays from Interest Payments
questions.prompt_template: In the government's intertemporal budget constraint Total Deficit_t = (G_t + TR_t - T_t) + rB_{t-1}, what does the primary deficit (D_t) measure?

hints.text: Notice the two bracketed terms in the total deficit equation: one reflects current program spending and taxes, the other reflects past debt.
Identify the term (G_t + TR_t - T_t) that excludes rB_{t-1}.

options_template.text: Non-interest government outlays (G_t + TR_t) minus tax revenues (T_t).
options_template.feedback: Correct. The primary deficit D_t = G_t + TR_t - T_t excludes interest payments on inherited debt so analysts can evaluate current taxing and spending decisions separately from past borrowing.

options_template.text: Total federal outlays including net interest payments minus tax revenues.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total vs. Primary Confusion): Including net interest payments (rB_{t-1}) gives the total budget deficit, not the primary deficit.

options_template.text: Net interest outlays on existing public debt alone (rB_{t-1}).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Interest-Component Isolation): rB_{t-1} is the debt-service interest component; the primary deficit captures non-interest fiscal policy choices.

options_template.text: The ratio of total public debt to nominal GDP (B_t / Y_t).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ratio Confusion): B_t / Y_t is the Debt-to-GDP ratio (b_t), a stock-to-flow sustainability measure rather than the primary deficit flow.

questions.title: Expansionary Fiscal Policy in a Recessionary Gap
questions.prompt_template: In the AD–AS model, an economy is initially in a short-run equilibrium at Y1 < Yp (a recessionary gap) along an upward-sloping SRAS curve. If Congress enacts expansionary fiscal policy (ΔG > 0 or ΔT < 0), how do the curves and equilibrium adjust in the short run?

hints.text: Determine which curve (AD, SRAS, or LRAS) responds immediately to higher government purchases or lower personal taxes.
Trace the new intersection of AD2 with an upward-sloping SRAS1 curve to see how both Y and P move.

options_template.text: SRAS shifts rightward while AD remains fixed, raising real GDP and lowering the price level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Shift Confusion): Standard demand-side fiscal stimulus shifts the AD curve, not the SRAS curve, in the short run.

options_template.text: AD shifts rightward, moving equilibrium up along SRAS so both real GDP and the price level rise.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Expansionary fiscal policy shifts AD1 rightward to AD2; moving up along SRAS1 closes the recessionary gap (Y1 -> Yp) while lifting the price level (P1 -> P2).

options_template.text: AD shifts leftward, moving equilibrium down along SRAS so real GDP falls further below Yp.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift Direction Reversal): A leftward shift of AD results from contractionary fiscal policy, not expansionary policy.

options_template.text: LRAS shifts leftward to meet Y1, eliminating the recessionary gap without changing the price level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Potential-Output Misconception): Expansionary demand policy closes a recessionary gap by moving actual output up toward Yp, not by reducing potential output LRAS.

questions.title: Contractionary Fiscal Policy in an Inflationary Gap
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy is initially in an inflationary gap with Y1 > Yp. To close the gap, Congress enacts contractionary fiscal policy (ΔG < 0 or ΔT > 0). What happens in the AD–AS diagram?

hints.text: When the economy is overheating (Y1 > Yp), policymakers want to cool total spending.
Trace the movement along an upward-sloping SRAS curve when AD shifts to the left.

options_template.text: AD shifts rightward, pushing equilibrium real GDP even further above Yp.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Reversal): Cutting G or raising T reduces planned spending and shifts AD leftward, not rightward.

options_template.text: SRAS shifts leftward, lowering real GDP to Yp while pushing the price level even higher.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curve Misidentification): Contractionary fiscal policy shifts AD leftward (reducing P), whereas a leftward SRAS shift represents a negative supply shock (stagflation).

options_template.text: AD shifts leftward, moving equilibrium down along SRAS so real GDP falls toward Yp and the price level moderates from P1 to P2.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Contractionary fiscal policy cools excess demand by shifting AD1 leftward to AD2, reducing both output (closing Y1 - Yp) and upward price pressure.

options_template.text: Both AD and SRAS shift rightward simultaneously, keeping the price level constant at P1.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dual-Shift Error): Contractionary fiscal policy contracts aggregate demand rather than shifting both AD and SRAS rightward.

questions.topic: Horizontal AD Shift vs. Short-Run Output Change
questions.title: Why Upward-Sloping SRAS Dampens the Multiplier
questions.prompt_template: Suppose MPC = 0.75 (so kG = 4) and government purchases rise by ΔG = +$100 billion. In an AD–AS diagram with an upward-sloping SRAS curve, how does the short-run increase in equilibrium real GDP (ΔY_SR) compare to $400 billion?

hints.text: Distinguish the horizontal distance between AD1 and AD2 at price P1 from the horizontal distance between equilibria E1 and E2.
Because SRAS slopes upward, E2 lies at a higher price level P2 than E1, which moves the economy upward-left along AD2.

options_template.text: ΔY_SR equals exactly $400 billion because the Keynesian multiplier fully determines equilibrium output regardless of price-level changes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Price Assumption Error): The simple multiplier $400B measures the horizontal shift of AD at a fixed price level; it equals ΔY_SR only if SRAS is completely horizontal.

options_template.text: ΔY_SR is strictly greater than $400 billion because rising prices stimulate extra household consumption.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Level Effect Reversal): Rising prices reduce real wealth, raise interest rates, and reduce net exports, which dampens rather than amplifies real output.

options_template.text: ΔY_SR is zero in the short run because nominal wages adjust instantaneously to keep output at Yp.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run vs. Long-Run Conflation): Zero real output gain occurs only along the vertical LRAS curve in the long run, not along an upward-sloping SRAS curve.

options_template.text: ΔY_SR is strictly less than $400 billion because the rightward shift of AD pushes up the price level, causing an upward-left movement along AD2.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Although AD shifts horizontally right by kG·ΔG = $400B at P1, moving up the upward-sloping SRAS curve raises P from P1 to P2, partially offsetting the real output gain so ΔY_SR < $400B.

questions.title: Fiscal Stimulus Near Full Employment
questions.prompt_template: In the AD–AS model, as an economy approaches or exceeds potential output (Yp), the effective SRAS curve becomes steeper. What does this imply graphically for an additional round of expansionary fiscal stimulus?

hints.text: Sketch a steep SRAS curve and shift AD rightward by a fixed horizontal distance.
Compare the vertical rise in P with the horizontal gain in Y when the supply curve is nearly vertical.

options_template.text: A rightward AD shift generates progressively larger increases in the price level and smaller gains in real GDP.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When resources and labor markets are tight near or above Yp, steeper SRAS means extra aggregate demand bids up wages and prices much more than it expands real production.

options_template.text: A rightward AD shift produces a larger increase in real GDP and almost no change in the price level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Flat-SRAS Confusion): Large output gains with minimal inflation occur only on the flat portion of SRAS during deep recessions, not on the steep portion near capacity.

options_template.text: The AD curve becomes vertical, eliminating any change in either prices or output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curve-Slope Swap): Capacity constraints steepen SRAS (and LRAS is vertical), not the AD curve.

options_template.text: SRAS automatically shifts rightward by the same distance as AD, keeping inflation at zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic Supply Expansion): Higher aggregate demand near full employment creates inflationary pressure rather than automatically expanding short-run supply.

questions.title: Equal-Dollar Spending Cut vs. Tax Hike on the AD Curve
questions.prompt_template: Compare two contractionary policies of identical dollar size: Policy X cuts government purchases by $50 billion (ΔG = -$50B), while Policy Y raises lump-sum taxes by $50 billion (ΔT = +$50B). Assuming 0 < MPC < 1, how do their horizontal shifts of the AD curve compare?

hints.text: First confirm the direction of both shifts: do ΔG < 0 and ΔT > 0 both contract aggregate demand?
Next compare the magnitudes of kG·(-50) and kT·(+50) when 0 < c < 1.

options_template.text: Both shift AD leftward by the exact same horizontal distance because both reduce the budget deficit by $50 billion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equal-Multiplier Fallacy): Equal deficit reductions do not yield equal AD shifts because a tax hike is partially absorbed by reduced household saving rather than reduced consumption.

options_template.text: Both shift AD leftward, and Policy X (ΔG = -$50B) shifts AD further to the left than Policy Y (ΔT = +$50B).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Both policies are contractionary (leftward AD shift), and because |kG| = 1/(1 - c) > |kT| = c/(1 - c), a $50B spending cut produces a larger leftward shift than a $50B tax hike.

options_template.text: Policy Y shifts AD further to the left than Policy X because taxes directly reduce household wealth.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplier Ranking Reversal): Households reduce consumption by only c·ΔT in Round 1, making the tax shift strictly smaller than the direct spending shift.

options_template.text: Policy X shifts AD leftward while Policy Y shifts AD rightward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error on Taxes): Raising taxes lowers disposable income and consumption, which shifts AD leftward just like a spending cut.

questions.title: Effect of a Proportional Income Tax on the AE Line
questions.prompt_template: In the Keynesian Cross (Planned AE vs. Real GDP) diagram, how does replacing a lump-sum tax with a proportional income tax T = T0 + tY (where 0 < t < 1) change the slope of the Planned AE line?

hints.text: Write disposable income with a proportional tax: YD = Y - (T0 + tY) + TR.
Substitute YD into C = C0 + c·YD and read off the coefficient multiplying Y.

options_template.text: It steepens the Planned AE line from slope c to slope c(1 + t).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error in Disposable Income): Taxes reduce disposable income to (1 - t)Y, not (1 + t)Y, so the slope decreases rather than increases.

options_template.text: It leaves the slope unchanged at c and only shifts the vertical intercept downward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lump-Sum vs. Proportional Confusion): Only a change in lump-sum taxes T0 shifts the vertical intercept without changing the slope; a proportional rate t alters the slope.

options_template.text: It flattens the Planned AE line from slope c to slope c(1 - t).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because each additional dollar of GDP yields only (1 - t) dollars of disposable income, induced consumption per dollar of GDP falls from c to c(1 - t), flattening the AE line.

options_template.text: It rotates the 45-degree AE = Y reference line downward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reference-Line Error): The 45-degree line is a geometric equilibrium condition (AE = Y) whose slope is always 1 regardless of tax policy.

questions.title: Comparing Autonomous Shocks on Steep vs. Flat AE Lines
questions.prompt_template: Two economies start at the same equilibrium GDP Y* in the Keynesian Cross diagram. Economy A has lump-sum taxes (steeper AE slope = c), while Economy B has proportional income taxes (flatter AE slope = c(1 - t)). If private investment drops vertically by ΔIp = -$100B in both economies, what does the diagram show?

hints.text: Visualize shifting both a steep line and a flat line downward by the exact same vertical distance and finding where each crosses the 45-degree line.
Remember that a smaller slope of AE corresponds to a smaller multiplier 1 / [1 - c(1 - t)].

options_template.text: Economy B experiences a larger horizontal drop in equilibrium real GDP than Economy A.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Multiplier Reversal): A flatter AE line means a smaller multiplier, not a larger one; the steeper line produces the larger horizontal GDP swing.

options_template.text: Both economies experience the exact same -$100B drop in equilibrium real GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplier Omission): Both economies have multipliers greater than 1 (as long as c(1 - t) > 0), and Economy A's steeper slope amplifies the shock more than Economy B's.

options_template.text: Economy B's equilibrium real GDP rises because tax revenues fall.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Over-Stabilization Fallacy): Automatic stabilizers dampen a negative shock so GDP falls less, but they cannot turn a negative investment shock into an economic expansion.

options_template.text: Economy B experiences a smaller horizontal drop in equilibrium real GDP than Economy A.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A flatter AE line intersects the 45-degree line closer to the original Y* after a given vertical shift, reflecting the smaller automatic-stabilizer multiplier kG^auto < kG.

questions.topic: Balanced-Budget Shift in the Keynesian Cross
questions.title: Vertical Shift of Planned AE Under a Balanced-Budget Expansion
questions.prompt_template: In the Keynesian Cross diagram with lump-sum taxes, Congress increases government purchases by ΔG = +$100B and raises lump-sum taxes by ΔT = +$100B simultaneously. How does the Planned AE line shift?

hints.text: Find the change in the vertical intercept of AE = C0 - cT + cTR + Ip + G + NX0 + cY when ΔG = ΔT = +$100B.
Compute Δ(G - cT) = (1 - c)ΔG and multiply by 1/(1 - c) to get ΔY*.

options_template.text: It shifts vertically upward by (1 - c) × $100B, raising equilibrium Y* by exactly $100B.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The net vertical shift of AE is ΔG - cΔT = (1 - c)ΔG > 0; multiplying this vertical shift by kG = 1/(1 - c) yields ΔY* = +$100B.

options_template.text: It does not shift at all because +ΔG and +ΔT cancel out in the vertical intercept.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Offset Fallacy): ΔG shifts AE up by +$100B, while ΔT shifts AE down by only -c($100B), leaving a positive net upward shift.

options_template.text: It shifts vertically upward by $100B, raising equilibrium Y* by $100B / (1 - c).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Tax Offset): A vertical shift of +$100B occurs only if ΔG is deficit-financed (ΔT = 0); the accompanying tax hike reduces C by c·ΔT.

options_template.text: It pivots downward to a flatter slope because higher lump-sum taxes reduce the MPC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope vs. Intercept Confusion): Lump-sum taxes change the vertical intercept of AE, not its slope c.

questions.title: Deficit Borrowing Shift in the Loanable Funds Market
questions.prompt_template: In the loanable funds market diagram (real interest rate r on the vertical axis, quantity of loanable funds on the horizontal axis), how is a deficit-financed fiscal expansion represented when S_private is held fixed?

hints.text: When the U.S. Treasury issues bonds to cover a deficit, is it supplying loanable funds or demanding loanable funds?
Trace the new intersection of D2 = I + Deficit with the upward-sloping S_private curve.

options_template.text: Demand for loanable funds shifts leftward, lowering the real interest rate from r1 to r2.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift Direction Reversal): A budget deficit increases total borrowing demand in credit markets, shifting demand rightward and raising r.

options_template.text: Demand for loanable funds shifts rightward from D1 = I to D2 = I + Deficit, raising the equilibrium real interest rate from r1 to r2.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Treasury borrowing adds to private investment demand, shifting demand rightward from D1 to D2 and driving up the equilibrium real interest rate from r1 to r2.

options_template.text: Private saving supply S_private shifts rightward by the full amount of the deficit, leaving r unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic Saving Offset): In the standard crowding-out model, Treasury borrowing increases demand for funds against an upward-sloping S_private, pushing r upward.

options_template.text: The real interest rate is fixed horizontally, so private investment rises alongside government borrowing.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Rate-Response Error): With an upward-sloping supply of private saving, higher demand raises r and crowds out—rather than crowds in—private investment.

questions.topic: Reading Crowding Out on the Loanable Funds Graph
questions.title: Distinguishing Total Borrowing from Crowded-Out Private Investment
questions.prompt_template: In the loanable funds diagram, deficit-financed borrowing shifts demand from D1 = I to D2 = I + Deficit, raising the real interest rate from r1 to r2 and total equilibrium loanable funds from I1 to Q2. Where on the graph is the new level of private investment (I2) located?

hints.text: Which curve represents private firms' investment demand alone, excluding government deficit borrowing?
Start at the new equilibrium real interest rate r2 on the vertical axis and move horizontally to the D1 = I curve.

options_template.text: At Q2 on the new demand curve D2, showing that private investment rose.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total vs. Private Borrowing Confusion): Q2 is total borrowing (private investment plus the federal deficit); private investment alone must be read off D1 = I.

options_template.text: At the horizontal distance between I1 and Q2 along the horizontal axis.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Saving-Response Confusion): The distance (Q2 - I1) measures the increase in private saving induced by the higher real interest rate, not crowded-out investment.

options_template.text: Directly on the original private investment demand curve D1 at the higher real interest rate r2, where I2 < I1.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At the higher interest rate r2, businesses move upward-left along D1 = I to I2 < I1; the horizontal distance (I1 - I2) measures the private investment crowded out.

options_template.text: At I1, because private investment depends only on real GDP and not on the real interest rate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Interest-Insensitivity Fallacy): Because D1 = I slopes downward with respect to r, a rise from r1 to r2 strictly reduces private investment from I1 to I2.

questions.title: When Crowding Out Is Weakest vs. Strongest
questions.prompt_template: Based on the loanable funds and AD–AS frameworks, under which macroeconomic condition does deficit-financed expansionary fiscal policy suffer the LEAST crowding out?

hints.text: Think about when Treasury borrowing competes aggressively with private firms for scarce savings versus when private demand for credit is depressed.
Compare credit-market conditions during a deep recession (near-zero interest rates) against an economy at full employment.

options_template.text: During an overheating boom when the economy operates above potential GDP and credit markets are tight.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Business-Cycle Reversal): Near or above full employment with tight credit markets, additional Treasury borrowing pushes r up sharply, causing maximum crowding out.

options_template.text: Whenever the marginal propensity to consume is zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplier Confusion): If MPC = 0, the fiscal multiplier is only 1 regardless of interest rates; crowding out depends on credit-market slack and interest-rate sensitivity.

options_template.text: Whenever the federal government finances spending entirely with lump-sum tax hikes instead of borrowing, which increases interest rates.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financing-Channel Error): Tax-financed spending does not require deficit borrowing in the loanable funds market, so it does not raise interest rates through Treasury bond issuance.

options_template.text: During a deep recession when private investment demand is weak and interest rates are near zero.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When credit markets have ample slack, private borrowing demand is depressed, and interest rates are near zero, government borrowing puts minimal upward pressure on r, yielding the strongest fiscal multiplier.

questions.topic: Transfer Payments in AE and AD Diagrams
questions.title: Graphical Impact of an Increase in Government Transfers
questions.prompt_template: When the federal government increases transfer payments by ΔTR > 0 (holding G, T, and the price level constant), how do the Planned AE line and the AD curve shift?

hints.text: Check how TR enters AE = C0 + c(Y - T + TR) + Ip + G + NX0.
The vertical shift of AE is the Round 1 change in consumption (+c·ΔTR); multiply that by 1/(1 - c) for the horizontal AD shift.

options_template.text: Planned AE shifts vertically upward by +c·ΔTR, and AD shifts horizontally rightward by +[c/(1 - c)]·ΔTR.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher transfers raise disposable income by ΔTR, lifting Round 1 consumption (the vertical AE intercept) by +c·ΔTR; multiplying by 1/(1 - c) gives a horizontal AD shift of +[c/(1 - c)]·ΔTR.

options_template.text: Planned AE shifts vertically upward by +ΔTR, and AD shifts horizontally rightward by +[1/(1 - c)]·ΔTR.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direct-Purchases Conflation): That formula applies to direct government purchases ΔG; households save (1 - c) of a transfer payment in Round 1.

options_template.text: Planned AE shifts vertically downward by -c·ΔTR, and AD shifts horizontally leftward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error): Transfer payments add to household disposable income (YD = Y - T + TR), so higher transfers shift AE upward and AD rightward.

options_template.text: Neither Planned AE nor AD shifts because transfers are not included in G.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Exclusion Fallacy): Although transfers are not part of G, they raise household disposable income and therefore increase consumption C.

questions.topic: Short-Run vs. Long-Run Effects of Public Infrastructure
questions.title: Dual Shift from Productive Public Infrastructure Investment
questions.prompt_template: Suppose the federal government finances productive public infrastructure—such as modernized bridges, ports, and power grids—through direct government purchases (ΔG > 0). How is this represented across the short run and long run in the AD–AS model?

hints.text: Separate the immediate spending effect (building the infrastructure) from the lasting capacity effect (using the finished infrastructure).
Building raises G (AD right); better bridges, ports, and grids raise potential output Yp (LRAS right).

options_template.text: AD shifts leftward in the short run while LRAS shifts leftward in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Reversal): Infrastructure spending raises G (shifting AD right) and enhances productive capital (shifting LRAS right).

options_template.text: AD shifts rightward in the short run, and higher productive capacity also shifts LRAS rightward in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Public infrastructure purchases immediately boost short-run aggregate demand (AD right) and, once completed, raise economy-wide productivity and potential output (LRAS right).

options_template.text: Only SRAS shifts rightward in the short run; AD and LRAS are completely unaffected.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Omission Error): Direct federal construction spending immediately enters G in AD = C + I + G + NX, and lasting infrastructure expands long-run potential output Yp.

options_template.text: LRAS shifts rightward immediately in Round 1, eliminating any short-run shift in AD.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Timing Error): Construction outlays boost AD first, whereas physical infrastructure expands LRAS only as projects are completed and put into service.

questions.title: Computing Horizontal AD Shift from Higher Government Purchases
questions.prompt_template: In a closed economy with lump-sum taxes and a fixed short-run price level, the marginal propensity to consume is c = 0.80. If the federal government increases direct purchases by ΔG = +$60 billion, what is the total horizontal shift in aggregate demand (ΔAD)?

hints.text: First compute the government purchases multiplier kG = 1 / (1 - c).
With c = 0.80, kG = 1 / 0.20 = 5; now multiply kG by ΔG = +$60 billion.

options_template.text: +$240 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Multiplier Substitution): $240 billion uses |kT| = c/(1 - c) = 4 instead of kG = 1/(1 - c) = 5.

options_template.text: +$75 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reciprocal-of-MPC Error): $75 billion divides $60 billion by c = 0.80 (1/0.80 = 1.25) instead of by MPS = 1 - c = 0.20.

options_template.text: +$300 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. With c = 0.80, kG = 1/(1 - 0.80) = 5, so ΔAD = 5 × $60 billion = +$300 billion.

options_template.text: +$48 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Round-2-Only Confusion): $48 billion computes c × $60 billion (only the induced spending in Round 2) instead of the cumulative multiplier effect.

questions.title: Computing Horizontal AD Shift from a Lump-Sum Tax Cut
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy has lump-sum taxes, a fixed short-run price level, and an MPC of c = 0.75. If Congress enacts a lump-sum tax cut of $80 billion (ΔT = -$80 billion), what is the resulting horizontal shift in aggregate demand (ΔAD)?

hints.text: Use the lump-sum tax multiplier kT = -c / (1 - c) and remember that a tax cut means ΔT < 0.
With c = 0.75, kT = -0.75 / 0.25 = -3; multiply -3 by ΔT = -$80 billion.

options_template.text: +$320 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Purchases-Multiplier Substitution): $320 billion applies kG = 4 instead of kT = -c/(1 - c) = -3, ignoring the 25% saved in Round 1.

options_template.text: -$240 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error on Tax Cut): A tax cut (ΔT = -$80B) increases disposable income and expands AD: (-3) × (-$80B) = +$240B, not -$240B.

options_template.text: +$60 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Round-1-Only Error): +$60 billion equals c × $80 billion (Round 1 consumption only) and omits all subsequent multiplier rounds.

options_template.text: +$240 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. The lump-sum tax multiplier is kT = -0.75 / (1 - 0.75) = -3, so ΔAD = (-3) × (-$80 billion) = +$240 billion.

questions.title: Tracing Round 2 of a Lump-Sum Tax Cut
questions.prompt_template: Suppose MPC = 0.80 and Congress enacts a lump-sum tax cut of $50 billion (ΔT = -$50 billion). Following the round-by-round spending cascade, how much additional spending is generated specifically in Round 2?

hints.text: Start with Round 1 of a tax cut: households spend fraction c of the $50B tax cut and save (1 - c).
Multiply Round 1 spending ($40B) by c = 0.80 again to find Round 2 spending (c² × $50B).

options_template.text: $32.0 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. In Round 1, households spend c × $50B = $40.0B; in Round 2, recipients of that income spend c × $40.0B = c² × $50B = 0.64 × $50B = $32.0 billion.

options_template.text: $40.0 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Round-1 Shift Error): $40.0 billion (0.80 × $50B) is Round 1 spending for a tax cut (or Round 2 for direct purchases ΔG), not Round 2 of a tax cut.

options_template.text: $25.6 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Round-3 Overshoot): $25.6 billion equals c³ × $50B, which is Round 3 spending rather than Round 2.

options_template.text: $50.0 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Saving-Leakage Error): Assuming $50.0 billion is spent in Round 1 applies to direct government purchases ΔG, not a tax cut where 20% is saved initially.

questions.title: Required Government Purchases to Close a Recessionary Gap
questions.prompt_template: An economy with lump-sum taxes and a fixed short-run price level has potential real GDP Yp = $22,000 billion, current equilibrium GDP Y0 = $21,200 billion, and MPC = 0.80. What change in government purchases (ΔG) is required to close the recessionary gap completely?

hints.text: First find the recessionary output gap: Yp - Y0.
Compute kG = 1 / (1 - 0.80) = 5, then solve ΔY = kG · ΔG for ΔG.

options_template.text: +$200 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Multiplier Division): +$200 billion divides the $800B gap by |kT| = 4 instead of kG = 5.

options_template.text: +$160 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. The recessionary gap is $22,000B - $21,200B = $800B. With kG = 1/(1 - 0.80) = 5, the required increase is ΔG = $800B / 5 = +$160 billion.

options_template.text: +$800 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplier Omission): Spending the full $800 billion ignores the multiplier and would shift AD by $4,000 billion, massively overshooting Yp.

options_template.text: +$640 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MPC-Multiplication Error): +$640 billion multiplies the $800B gap by c = 0.80 instead of dividing by kG = 5.

questions.title: Required Lump-Sum Tax Hike to Close an Inflationary Gap
questions.prompt_template: An overheating economy with lump-sum taxes and a fixed short-run price level has current equilibrium output Y0 = $18,600 billion, potential GDP Yp = $18,000 billion, and MPC = 0.75. What change in lump-sum taxes (ΔT) is needed to eliminate the inflationary gap?

hints.text: Since Y0 > Yp, policymakers need a negative change in output: ΔY = Yp - Y0 = -$600 billion.
Compute kT = -0.75 / 0.25 = -3, then solve -$600B = (-3) · ΔT.

options_template.text: +$150 billion (a tax increase of $150 billion)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Purchases-Multiplier Division): +$150 billion divides $600B by kG = 4 rather than |kT| = 3; a $150B tax hike reduces AD by only $450B.

options_template.text: -$200 billion (a tax cut of $200 billion)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy Direction Reversal): Cutting taxes expands AD by +$600B, doubling the inflationary gap instead of closing it.

options_template.text: +$200 billion (a tax increase of $200 billion)
options_template.feedback: Correct. To close the $600B inflationary gap, policymakers need ΔY = -$600B. With kT = -0.75/(1 - 0.75) = -3, ΔT = (-$600B) / (-3) = +$200 billion.

options_template.text: +$450 billion (a tax increase of $450 billion)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MPC-Multiplication Error): Multiplying the $600B gap by c = 0.75 yields $450B, which would contract AD by $1,350B and trigger a recession.

questions.title: Computing AD Expansion from Higher Government Transfers
questions.prompt_template: In an economy with lump-sum taxes and MPC = 0.60, the federal government increases transfer payments by ΔTR = +$120 billion. Assuming a fixed short-run price level, what is the resulting horizontal shift in aggregate demand (ΔAD)?

hints.text: Recall that transfers have the same magnitude multiplier as lump-sum taxes, with a positive sign: kTR = c / (1 - c).
Evaluate kTR = 0.60 / 0.40 = 1.5, then multiply by ΔTR = +$120 billion.

options_template.text: +$300 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Purchases-Multiplier Substitution): +$300 billion uses kG = 1/0.40 = 2.5 instead of kTR = c/(1 - c) = 1.5.

options_template.text: +$72 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Round-1-Only Error): +$72 billion equals 0.60 × $120 billion, capturing only Round 1 consumption and omitting subsequent rounds.

options_template.text: +$120 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unit-Multiplier Assumption): Assuming kTR = 1 ignores both Round 1 saving leakage and secondary spending rounds.

options_template.text: +$180 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. With c = 0.60, the transfer multiplier is kTR = 0.60 / (1 - 0.60) = 1.5, so ΔAD = 1.5 × $120 billion = +$180 billion.

questions.title: Calculating Net AD Shift of a Balanced-Budget Expansion
questions.prompt_template: Suppose MPC = 0.80 and taxes are lump-sum. Congress increases federal purchases by ΔG = +$90 billion and finances the entire outlay by raising lump-sum taxes by ΔT = +$90 billion. What is the net horizontal shift in aggregate demand (ΔAD)?

hints.text: Compute the separate effects of ΔG = +$90B (using kG) and ΔT = +$90B (using kT), then add them.
Alternatively, apply the balanced-budget multiplier identity kBB = kG + kT = 1 directly.

options_template.text: +$90 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. The spending boost is 5 × $90B = +$450B and the tax contraction is (-4) × $90B = -$360B, leaving a net shift of +$90 billion (kBB = 1).

options_template.text: $0 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Complete-Offset Fallacy): Equal increases in G and T do not cancel out because kG = 5 exceeds |kT| = 4.

options_template.text: +$450 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Tax Contraction): +$450 billion counts only kG × $90B = 5 × $90B and omits the -$360B contraction from the tax hike.

options_template.text: +$810 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign-Error Summation): +$810 billion adds |kG| + |kT| = 9 instead of subtracting the contractionary tax effect.

questions.title: Net AD Shift from Simultaneous Spending Increase and Tax Cut
questions.prompt_template: In an economy with lump-sum taxes and MPC = 0.75, Congress passes a stimulus package that increases government purchases by ΔG = +$100 billion AND cuts lump-sum taxes by $40 billion (ΔT = -$40 billion). What is the total horizontal shift in aggregate demand (ΔAD)?

hints.text: Compute the horizontal AD shift from ΔG and from ΔT separately using kG = 1/(1 - c) and kT = -c/(1 - c).
With c = 0.75, kG = 4 and kT = -3; carefully check the double negative in (-3) × (-$40B).

options_template.text: +$280 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Cut Sign Reversal): +$280 billion subtracts $120B from $400B, treating the tax cut as if it were a tax hike.

options_template.text: +$520 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. With kG = 4 and kT = -3, ΔAD = 4($100B) + (-3)(-$40B) = +$400B + $120B = +$520 billion.

options_template.text: +$560 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uniform-Multiplier Error): +$560 billion applies kG = 4 to both the $100B spending hike and the $40B tax cut (4 × $140B).

options_template.text: +$140 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplier Omission): +$140 billion simply sums the raw dollar changes ($100B + $40B) without applying fiscal multipliers.

questions.title: Output Drop Under an Automatic Income Tax Stabilizer
questions.prompt_template: An economy has MPC = 0.75 and a proportional income tax rate of t = 0.20 (T = T0 + 0.20Y). If autonomous private investment falls by ΔIp = -$80 billion at a fixed price level, by how much does equilibrium real GDP change?

hints.text: Use the automatic-stabilizer multiplier formula kG^auto = 1 / [1 - c(1 - t)].
Compute c(1 - t) = 0.75 × 0.80 = 0.60, so kG^auto = 1 / 0.40 = 2.5, then multiply by -$80 billion.

options_template.text: -$320 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Proportional Tax): -$320 billion uses the lump-sum multiplier kG = 1/(1 - 0.75) = 4, ignoring the tax rate t = 0.20.

options_template.text: -$120 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Transfer-Multiplier Formula Error): -$120 billion uses c(1 - t)/[1 - c(1 - t)] = 1.5 instead of 1/[1 - c(1 - t)] = 2.5.

options_template.text: -$200 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. The proportional-tax multiplier is kG^auto = 1 / [1 - 0.75(1 - 0.20)] = 1 / (1 - 0.60) = 2.5, so ΔY = 2.5 × (-$80 billion) = -$200 billion.

options_template.text: -$100 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted MPC): -$100 billion uses 1/(1 - t) = 1.25, omitting c = 0.75 from the denominator.

questions.title: Computing Total Deficit and End-of-Year Public Debt
questions.prompt_template: A country begins the fiscal year with public debt B_{t-1} = $10,000 billion and pays a nominal interest rate of r = 4% on its debt. During the year, non-interest outlays are G_t + TR_t = $4,500 billion and tax revenues are T_t = $4,200 billion. What are the total budget deficit and end-of-year public debt (B_t)?

hints.text: Use Total Deficit_t = (G_t + TR_t - T_t) + rB_{t-1}.
Add the primary deficit ($300B) and interest payments (4% of $10,000B = $400B), then add the total deficit to B_{t-1}.

options_template.text: Total deficit = $300 billion; end-of-year debt = $10,300 billion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Interest Outlays): $300 billion is only the primary deficit (4,500 - 4,200); it omits the $400 billion in interest payments on existing debt.

options_template.text: Total deficit = $400 billion; end-of-year debt = $10,400 billion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Interest-Only Error): $400 billion counts only net interest outlays and ignores the $300 billion primary deficit.

options_template.text: Total deficit = $100 billion; end-of-year debt = $10,100 billion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Primary-Interest Subtraction): Subtracting the $300B primary deficit from the $400B interest cost treats a primary deficit as if it were a primary surplus.

options_template.text: Total deficit = $700 billion; end-of-year debt = $10,700 billion.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Primary deficit D_t = $4,500B - $4,200B = $300B, and interest outlays rB_{t-1} = 0.04 × $10,000B = $400B. Total deficit = $700B, raising debt to B_t = $10,700 billion.

questions.title: Primary Balance Required to Stabilize Debt-to-GDP When r > g
questions.prompt_template: A nation enters the year with a Debt-to-GDP ratio of b_{t-1} = 120% (1.20), an average nominal interest rate on public debt of r = 5.0%, and a nominal GDP growth rate of g = 3.5%. Using the linear approximation Δb_t ≈ (r - g)b_{t-1} + d_t, what primary budget balance (d_t) is required to keep the Debt-to-GDP ratio constant (Δb_t = 0)?

hints.text: Compute the interest-growth differential (r - g) and multiply it by b_{t-1} = 1.20.
Set (0.050 - 0.035)(1.20) + d_t = 0 and solve for d_t; remember d_t < 0 indicates a primary surplus.

options_template.text: A primary budget surplus of 1.8% of GDP (d_t = -1.8%).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting 0 = (0.050 - 0.035)(1.20) + d_t gives 0 = +0.018 + d_t, so d_t = -0.018 (a primary budget surplus of 1.8% of GDP).

options_template.text: A primary budget deficit of 1.8% of GDP (d_t = +1.8%).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): Since r > g, interest compounding pushes b_t up by +1.8 percentage points; running a primary deficit would raise b_t further instead of stabilizing it.

options_template.text: A primary budget surplus of 1.5% of GDP (d_t = -1.5%).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Debt-Ratio Weight): 1.5% is just (r - g) alone; you must multiply (r - g) by the initial Debt-to-GDP ratio b_{t-1} = 1.20.

options_template.text: A primary budget surplus of 6.0% of GDP (d_t = -6.0%).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored GDP Growth): 6.0% equals r × b_{t-1} = 5.0% × 1.20, ignoring the denominator growth g = 3.5% that helps erode the debt ratio.

questions.title: Computing Change in Debt-to-GDP Ratio Under Rapid Growth
questions.prompt_template: An economy has an initial Debt-to-GDP ratio of b_{t-1} = 80% (0.80), a nominal interest rate on debt of r = 3.0%, a nominal GDP growth rate of g = 5.5%, and a primary budget deficit of d_t = 1.0% of GDP (+0.010). Using Δb_t ≈ (r - g)b_{t-1} + d_t, how does the Debt-to-GDP ratio change this year?

hints.text: Substitute r = 0.030, g = 0.055, b_{t-1} = 0.80, and d_t = +0.010 into Δb_t ≈ (r - g)b_{t-1} + d_t.
Notice that (r - g) = -0.025 is negative; multiply by 0.80 to get -0.020 (-2.0 percentage points), then add +1.0 percentage point.

options_template.text: It rises by 3.0 percentage points (from 80.0% to 83.0%).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Differential Sign Reversal): +3.0 percentage points uses (g - r) instead of (r - g), mistakenly treating rapid GDP growth as increasing the debt ratio.

options_template.text: It falls by 1.0 percentage point (from 80.0% to 79.0%).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Δb_t ≈ (0.030 - 0.055)(0.80) + 0.010 = (-0.025)(0.80) + 0.010 = -0.020 + 0.010 = -0.010, so the Debt-to-GDP ratio declines by 1.0 percentage point.

options_template.text: It falls by 1.5 percentage points (from 80.0% to 78.5%).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Debt-Ratio Weight): -1.5 percentage points computes (3.0% - 5.5%) + 1.0% without multiplying (r - g) by b_{t-1} = 0.80.

options_template.text: It rises by 1.0 percentage point (from 80.0% to 81.0%).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Interest-Growth Term): Assuming Δb_t = d_t ignores the -2.0 percentage point erosion from g > r.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Multiplier Magnitude vs. Disbursement Speed Trade-Off
questions.prompt_template: Comparing the 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA) and the March 2020 CARES Act reveals a central design trade-off in fiscal policy. Which statement best summarizes this trade-off?

hints.text: Recall why ARRA infrastructure outlays rolled out over 2010–2011 while CARES Act payments arrived within weeks.
Weigh the theoretical multiplier advantage of ΔG against the implementation-speed advantage of ΔTR.

options_template.text: Direct infrastructure purchases disburse faster than electronic transfer checks, but have a smaller theoretical multiplier.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade-Off Reversal): Direct purchases have the larger theoretical multiplier (kG > kTR) but suffer longer implementation lags than electronic transfers.

options_template.text: Both packages relied exclusively on balanced-budget tax hikes so that federal debt would not rise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Historical Fact Error): Both ARRA ($787B) and the CARES Act were deficit-financed countercyclical stimulus packages, not balanced-budget tax hikes.

options_template.text: Direct infrastructure purchases (G) carry a larger theoretical multiplier than transfers, but transfers and expanded UI (TR) disburse far faster when an abrupt shock hits.
options_template.feedback: Correct. ARRA highway and clean-energy projects required engineering bids and environmental reviews (long implementation lag), whereas CARES Act stimulus checks and UI supplements reached households within weeks.

options_template.text: The CARES Act relied solely on state balanced-budget grants because federal transfers have a zero multiplier.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy Mischaracterization): The CARES Act prioritized direct federal household checks, expanded UI supplements, and forgivable small-business payroll loans, all of which carry positive multipliers.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Empirical Multiplier Differences Across Income Groups
questions.prompt_template: Empirical evaluations of the 2001 and 2008 tax rebates and the 2020–2021 Economic Impact Payments show that lower-income, liquidity-constrained households exhibit a much higher short-run MPC (c ≈ 0.70–0.90) than high-income households (c ≈ 0.10–0.25). What does this imply for designing short-run fiscal stimulus?

hints.text: Connect a higher MPC (c) among recipients to the size of Round 1 consumption and the transfer multiplier c/(1 - c).
Compare how liquidity-constrained households vs. affluent households with ample liquid savings use a temporary payment.

options_template.text: Across-the-board tax cuts for high-income earners deliver the largest immediate boost to aggregate demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MPC-Targeting Reversal): Because high-income households save most of a temporary tax rebate or pay down debt (low c), their short-run spending multiplier is much smaller.

options_template.text: Household income distribution has no effect on fiscal multipliers because the tax multiplier depends only on the federal deficit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Homogeneous-MPC Assumption): Because kT and kTR depend directly on the recipients' MPC, who receives the funds strongly alters the effective multiplier.

options_template.text: Targeting lower-income households reduces aggregate demand because they save 70%–90% of stimulus checks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MPC-MPS Swap): An MPC of 0.70–0.90 means households spend 70%–90% of additional income immediately and save only 10%–30%.

options_template.text: Targeted transfers such as SNAP, unemployment insurance, and income-phased rebates generate a substantially larger short-run demand multiplier per federal dollar.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Directing funds to liquidity-constrained households with higher MPC increases Round 1 consumption and amplifies kTR = c/(1 - c), yielding greater short-run bang per buck.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: How Discretionary Lags Can Turn Stimulus Procyclical
questions.prompt_template: Why can a well-intentioned discretionary fiscal stimulus package inadvertently destabilize the economy and fuel inflation?

hints.text: Think about the combined duration of recognition, legislative, and implementation lags relative to the length of a typical recession.
Ask what happens in the AD–AS model if a large rightward AD shift arrives after the recession has already ended.

options_template.text: Because recognition, legislative, and implementation lags can delay the spending until after the economy has already recovered near potential output.
options_template.feedback: Correct. If stimulus arrives once the economy has self-recovered to Yp, the rightward AD shift pushes output into an inflationary gap along the steep portion of SRAS.

options_template.text: Because discretionary stimulus automatically lowers the marginal income tax rate permanently to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Misconception): Discretionary stimulus bills do not permanently set income tax rates to zero; the destabilization risk comes from poor timing due to policy lags.

options_template.text: Because every dollar of discretionary spending shifts LRAS leftward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Destruction Fallacy): Fiscal stimulus shifts AD rightward; it does not destroy long-run productive capacity.

options_template.text: Because automatic stabilizers stop working whenever Congress passes a discretionary bill.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mutual-Exclusion Fallacy): Automatic stabilizers continue operating in standing law alongside discretionary measures.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Historical Lessons: 1968 Tax Surcharge vs. Mid-2021 Overheating
questions.prompt_template: In mid-2021, U.S. job openings exceeded unemployed workers while supply chains remained constrained and core inflation accelerated. How does the AD–AS framework explain both the risk of extra stimulus in mid-2021 and Congress's rationale for the 1968 10% income tax surcharge?

hints.text: Identify whether mid-2021 and 1968 represented recessionary gaps or inflationary gaps.
Recall how contractionary fiscal policy (like a tax surcharge) shifts AD to relieve demand-pull inflation.

options_template.text: In an inflationary gap, cutting taxes shifts SRAS rightward immediately, which was why Congress cut taxes by 10% in 1968.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Historical & Model Error): The 1968 Act enacted a 10% tax surcharge (increase), not a tax cut, specifically to shift AD leftward.

options_template.text: In an inflationary gap, extra expansionary stimulus pushes AD up the steep portion of SRAS (fueling inflation), whereas a temporary tax surcharge shifts AD leftward to cool demand-pull inflation.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When Y > Yp along a steep SRAS curve, more stimulus mainly bids up prices; conversely, the 1968 Revenue and Expenditure Control Act used contractionary taxation to shift AD left and restrain Vietnam-era inflation.

options_template.text: When job openings exceed unemployed workers, fiscal policy has no effect on the price level because SRAS is completely flat.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Inversion): Excess job openings and supply bottlenecks place the economy on the steep—not flat—portion of SRAS.

options_template.text: During supply-chain constraints, raising government purchases always lowers inflation by increasing consumer confidence.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Inflation Reversal): Adding aggregate demand when supply is constrained intensifies upward price pressure rather than lowering inflation.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why the Federal Deficit Shrank Sharply Between FY 2021 and FY 2022
questions.prompt_template: Between FY 2021 and FY 2022, the U.S. federal budget deficit shrank by more than half without Congress passing a single contractionary tax-hike bill. Which mechanism best explains this rapid deficit reduction?

hints.text: Ask how federal tax receipts and transfer outlays respond automatically during a strong nominal economic expansion.
Connect progressive income tax brackets and winding down emergency transfers to the shrinking cyclical deficit.

options_template.text: Balanced-budget rules forced the U.S. Treasury to cancel all outstanding Treasury bonds.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Error): The federal government has no constitutional balanced-budget rule and never canceled outstanding Treasury debt.

options_template.text: The Federal Reserve directly collected personal income taxes from households to pay down the deficit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Agency Confusion): Tax collection is performed by the IRS under federal tax law, not by the Federal Reserve.

options_template.text: Automatic stabilizers: rapid nominal wage, GDP, and capital-gains growth pushed taxpayers into higher progressive brackets while pandemic transfer outlays wound down.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Progressive income taxes automatically captured surging revenues during the 2021–2022 expansion while temporary transfer outlays expired, shrinking the deficit automatically.

options_template.text: A severe recession in 2022 reduced federal spending to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Macroeconomic Fact Error): FY 2021–2022 was a period of rapid nominal GDP and wage expansion, not a recession.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Offsetting a Cyclical Deficit During a Recession Is Counterproductive
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a sharp recession pushes real GDP well below potential (Y < Yp), causing the federal budget deficit to widen automatically due to lower tax receipts and higher unemployment claims. Why do macroeconomists warn against raising taxes or cutting spending to close this cyclical deficit immediately?

hints.text: Consult the policy interpretation for a recession (Y < Yp) in the cyclical vs. structural budget balance framework.
Trace what happens to AD and real GDP if Congress responds to a recession-induced deficit with contractionary tax hikes or spending cuts.

options_template.text: Because raising taxes during a recession increases the balanced-budget multiplier to infinity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Formula Distortion): The balanced-budget multiplier is always 1, and raising taxes alone (ΔT > 0) is strictly contractionary.

options_template.text: Because cyclical deficits never add to the national debt.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Accounting Error): Cyclical deficits do add to public debt in the short run, but economists still avoid procyclical austerity during recessions because it deepens the slump.

options_template.text: Because cutting government purchases during a recession raises real interest rates and increases crowding out.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Interest-Rate Direction Error): Cutting G reduces borrowing demand and lowers (not raises) interest rates; the danger is contracting AD when Y < Yp.

options_template.text: Because austerity measures shift AD further leftward, deepening the recessionary gap and potentially eroding tax revenues even further.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A cyclical deficit reflects automatic stabilizers cushioning household income; overriding them with contractionary austerity worsens unemployment and output losses.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting the Observed Budget Balance in an Inflationary Boom
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy is operating above potential output (Y > Yp) in an inflationary boom, and the observed federal budget deficit is $400 billion. What does this imply about the structural (cyclically adjusted) budget deficit?

hints.text: Recall the identity: Observed Balance = Structural Balance + Cyclical Balance.
During an expansion (Y > Yp), is the cyclical balance positive (surplus) or negative (deficit)? Solve for the structural balance.

options_template.text: The structural deficit is larger than $400 billion because the boom generates an automatic cyclical surplus that partially masks the underlying shortfall.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When Y > Yp, elevated tax receipts and low UI payouts create a cyclical surplus; once output returns to Yp, that cyclical cushion disappears, revealing a structural deficit larger than $400B.

options_template.text: The structural deficit is smaller than $400 billion because booms create automatic cyclical deficits.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cyclical-Sign Reversal): Economic expansions create automatic cyclical surpluses (higher tax receipts, lower transfers), not cyclical deficits.

options_template.text: The structural deficit equals exactly $400 billion because cyclical balances are always zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Cyclical-Balance Error): The cyclical balance is zero only when Y = Yp; when Y > Yp, the cyclical balance is in surplus.

options_template.text: The structural budget must be in surplus because observed deficits can only occur during recessions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Structural-Deficit Blindness): A country can easily run an observed deficit even during a boom if its baseline structural spending exceeds revenues.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Deficit Flow vs. Debt Stock Fallacy
questions.title: Interpreting a Narrowing Federal Deficit
questions.prompt_template: Suppose the U.S. federal budget deficit narrows from -$1,700 billion in FY 2025 to -$1,300 billion in FY 2026. Which statement about total public debt in FY 2026 is correct?

hints.text: Ask whether the federal government spent more than it collected in FY 2026.
A deficit of -$1,300B means $1,300B of net new Treasury borrowing during FY 2026.

options_template.text: Total public debt falls by $400 billion because the deficit was reduced by $400 billion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Flow-Change vs. Stock-Change Confusion): Reducing the deficit by $400B slows the pace of debt growth, but because the deficit is still negative (-$1,300B), debt still rises.

options_template.text: Total public debt still rises by $1,300 billion in FY 2026; public debt falls in dollar terms only when the government runs a budget surplus.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Any positive deficit represents net new borrowing added to the stock of debt; shrinking the deficit from $1,700B to $1,300B merely slows debt accumulation.

options_template.text: Total public debt remains unchanged because the deficit shrank.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Flow Error): Public debt remains unchanged only when the budget is exactly balanced ($0 deficit).

options_template.text: Total public debt rises by $3,000 billion in FY 2026 alone.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Two-Year Summation Error): $3,000 billion is the combined borrowing across both FY 2025 and FY 2026, not the increase in FY 2026 alone.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Proper Use of FRED Series FYFSD
