questions.prompt_template: An economics student downloads FRED series FYFSD (Federal Surplus or Deficit [-], annual by fiscal year, not seasonally adjusted) to compute the U.S. deficit-to-GDP ratio. Which methodological mistake must the student avoid?

hints.text: Recall the time period covered by FYFSD: it is an annual federal fiscal-year flow (October 1–September 30).
Think about what goes wrong when you divide an annual flow by a single unannualized quarter's output.

options_template.text: Treating negative values of FYFSD as budget deficits.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Correct Convention Misidentified): In FRED series FYFSD, negative values genuinely indicate budget deficits and positive values indicate surpluses.

options_template.text: Recognizing that FYFSD is reported in millions of dollars.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Correct Unit Misidentified): Checking that FYFSD is reported in millions of dollars is essential good practice so units match GDP.

options_template.text: Dividing annual fiscal-year FYFSD directly by a single calendar quarter's unannualized GDP without aligning fiscal years or matching time periods.
options_template.feedback: Correct. FYFSD is an annual flow measured over the federal fiscal year (October 1–September 30); dividing an annual flow by a single unannualized quarter's GDP distorts the ratio by roughly a factor of four and mismatches dates.

options_template.text: Distinguishing FYFSD (a flow variable) from gross federal debt (a stock variable).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Correct Concept Misidentified): Separating annual deficit flows (FYFSD) from the debt stock is exact macroeconomic best practice.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: How U.S. Debt-to-GDP Fell From Over 118% (1946) to ~31% (1981)
questions.prompt_template: Historical OMB records and FRED series GFDEGDQ188S show that the U.S. federal Debt-to-GDP ratio fell from over 118% in 1946 to roughly 31% by 1981, even though total nominal dollar debt increased over that period. How was this possible?

hints.text: Look at the fraction B_t / Y_t: how can a fraction fall even when its numerator B_t is rising?
Connect post-WWII de-leveraging to the debt dynamics condition g > r.

options_template.text: The U.S. government ran massive budget surpluses every single year between 1946 and 1981 to pay off all WWII bonds.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus Myth): The prompt explicitly notes that nominal dollar debt rose over 1946–1981; the ratio fell because denominator growth outpaced numerator growth.

options_template.text: The U.S. Treasury defaulted on its World War II debt obligations in the 1950s.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Historical Fact Error): The United States honored all WWII Treasury obligations in full; de-leveraging occurred through growth (g > r).

options_template.text: Deflation shrank nominal GDP faster than nominal debt.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ratio Arithmetic Error): Shrinking the denominator (nominal GDP) would raise the Debt-to-GDP ratio, not lower it.

options_template.text: Nominal GDP growth (g) consistently outpaced nominal interest compounding (r) and net debt accumulation, expanding the denominator faster than the numerator.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because strong real GDP growth and moderate inflation expanded nominal GDP (Y_t) much faster than nominal public debt (B_t) grew, the ratio B_t / Y_t fell by over 85 percentage points without large budget surpluses.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Structural Entitlements Under r > g
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an aging population steadily raises mandatory entitlement outlays (Social Security and Medicare), generating persistent structural primary deficits (d_t > 0), while average nominal interest rates on sovereign debt exceed nominal GDP growth (r > g). What does the Debt-to-GDP law of motion predict?

hints.text: Check the signs of both terms in Δb_t ≈ (r - g)b_{t-1} + d_t when r > g and d_t > 0.
When both terms are strictly positive, can Δb_t ever reach zero without changing taxes or spending?

options_template.text: The Debt-to-GDP ratio will climb continuously unless tax revenues or spending trajectories are adjusted to improve the primary balance.
options_template.feedback: Correct. With r > g and d_t > 0, both interest compounding and primary deficits push b_t upward every year; stabilizing b_t requires moving toward a primary surplus (d_t < 0).

options_template.text: The Debt-to-GDP ratio will automatically stabilize at 100% without any fiscal adjustments.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic-Stabilization Illusion): When both (r - g) > 0 and d_t > 0, Δb_t = (r - g)b_{t-1} + d_t is strictly positive and accelerating—there is no automatic cap at 100%.

options_template.text: The Debt-to-GDP ratio will fall as long as the primary deficit stays constant as a share of GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error): A constant positive primary deficit combined with r > g guarantees a rising—not falling—Debt-to-GDP ratio.

options_template.text: Higher entitlement spending immediately raises g above r, eliminating any debt sustainability concern.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unbounded-Growth Fallacy): Mandatory transfer outlays for an aging population do not automatically lift long-run GDP growth above interest rates.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Combining Automatic Stabilizers, Targeted Transfers, and Public Infrastructure
questions.prompt_template: Synthesizing the lessons of Chapter 10, how do modern macroeconomists recommend combining fiscal tools across a severe, persistent recession while maintaining long-run fiscal sustainability?

hints.text: Match each fiscal instrument to its comparative advantage: speed (zero lag), high short-run MPC, long-run LRAS growth, and debt sustainability.
Recall the Bring It Home conclusion: automatic stabilizers and discretionary tools act as complements, not substitutes.

options_template.text: Eliminate all automatic stabilizers so Congress must vote on every dollar of unemployment insurance during a recession.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lag-Amplification Error): Removing automatic stabilizers would expose the economy to severe recognition and legislative lags during downturns.

options_template.text: Rely on automatic stabilizers for immediate zero-lag cushioning, add targeted transfers to high-MPC households if the slump persists, and pair productive public infrastructure (ΔG) with a credible medium-run debt framework.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Automatic stabilizers act immediately and self-terminate; targeted transfers deliver rapid high-MPC support; productive infrastructure lifts both short-run AD and long-run LRAS; and a medium-run framework keeps B/Y sustainable.

options_template.text: Cut government purchases and raise taxes during the recession, then enact permanent deficit-financed stimulus during the next inflationary boom.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Procyclical Policy Reversal): Tightening during recessions and stimulating during booms amplifies rather than dampens business-cycle volatility.

options_template.text: Use exclusively across-the-board tax cuts for top earners during recessions and ignore long-run structural deficits entirely.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Low-MPC & Sustainability Neglect): Top-earner tax rebates have lower short-run MPCs, and ignoring persistent structural deficits risks an unsustainable Debt-to-GDP trajectory when r > g.
